newsitem.title: JAPAN: Some Japan traders hesitant to buy more Iraqi oil.
newsitem.headline: Some Japan traders hesitant to buy more Iraqi oil.

text.p: Even if Iraq were able to double the current export volumes allowed under the United Nations oil-for-food deal, some Japanese customers would be hesitant to increase their purchase volumes, oil traders said on Wednesday.

Iraq's chief negotiator of the oil-for food agreement, Abdul Amir al-Anbari, on Tuesday called on the U.N. to double the financing ceiling for Iraq's humanitarian oil sales to $4 billion over six months from $2 billion.
"While there may be plenty of room and desire here to take more Iraqi barrels, I just can't imagine Japan would step out of line politically," said one importer of Middle East grades.
"There's just no need for it," he added.

The United States has been a major critic of the Iraqi government and has threatened in recent weeks that Iraq could lose the oil-for-food deal if it does not fully meet its obligations under the deal.
The trader said this might discourage some Japanese customers from taking additional barrels if the sales ceiling were increased.
A total of seven Japanese oil companies have so far purchased substantial volumes of Iraq's Basrah Light grade for delivery in the oil deal's first six-months.

While U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan has said he expects the Security Council to renew the food-for-oil deal for another six-months beginning June 8, U.N. diplomats say the accord will likely roll over at the current $2 billion oil sales limit.

Another trader who imported Iraqi barrels on a trial basis in March said on Wednesday that while political considerations were a factor, unfavourable shipping economics made further purchases unappealing.

"We would not be interested in any additional Iraqi material at present," the trader said. "Not because of quality issues, but because of shipping costs involved with chartering vessels from second parties."
He added: "We are focused very sharply now on trimming shipping costs in order to improve our refinery profits."
Japanese refiners Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd and Cosmo Oil Co Ltd have purchased oil using their own vessels for the voyage from Iraq's Mina al-Bakr terminal in the Gulf, the trader said.
Other companies, with the exception of the most recent purchase by Nippon Oil Co Ltd, have imported Iraqi crude through trading house Mitsubishi Corp 8058 T.
Idemitsu seemed less concerned than some other firms with the political implications of future Iraqi purchases.
"It's all a matter of the price," a company spokesman said.
"If the price is favourable, and there's extra availability I think there's a chance (that we might purchase more)," he said.
A spokesman from Cosmo Oil said the company expected to continue its current purchase levels of roughly 10,000 barrels per day (bpd).
"We will adhere to the decision made by the Security Council," the spokesman said.
"We expect our volumes to be similar to those in the first 180 days of the deal," he said.

Under the oil sale accord, Iraq is permitted to sell $2 billion worth of crude over a six-month period to June 7 to buy food and medicine to alleviate hardship from sanctions imposed on Baghdad after it invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
